groups.title: Jokes and wordplay
groups.q: These lines contain a joke or a play on words. Does each one work in your language?

rows.text: That's just his factory setting.
rows.note: messing things up is simply his nature

rows.text: Forgiven. The whole boulevard is yours.
rows.note: in Persian, "forgive" also means "give away"

rows.text: until yesterday you said "ass." Now you've gone all civilized and say "donkey"?
rows.note: teasing a boy for switching to a politer word

rows.text: Pir-to-pir? … Eagle Eye says peer-to-peer; Taverny says Eldie-to-Eldie.
rows.note: he hears "peer" as Persian pir, "elder", the root of his nickname

rows.text: Last night I could hear you ruminating.
rows.note: chewing at night, like a cow chewing cud

rows.text: What the hell's wrong with you this time, getting it up at us, Alain Dickon?
rows.note: double meaning: sitting up proudly, and an erection

rows.text: What izer wasn't he?
rows.note: the mother catches only the end of "womanizer"

rows.text: The friend of the cousin of our brother-in-law's master craftsman who is the richest man in Tehran
rows.note: a boy's running boast

rows.text: Or you're dick-brai... well, you already were dick-brained, now you've become even more dick-brained.
rows.note: the insult is cut off, then made worse

rows.text: Yeah, all of us own factories. … We've got a bullshit factory.
rows.note: all they produce is bullshit: they just talk nonsense

rows.text: You fossil, you're a monument to stupidity and decline
rows.note: a mocking insult

rows.text: life is like a thousand-toman banknote: whichever side you look at, it smells of lentil rice.
rows.note: an absurd quip

rows.text: This is how I talk; you hear me speak, you think it's poetry.
rows.note: a boy answers in a sing-song rhythm

rows.text: Careful you don't crack, Mr. Dick.
rows.note: he has just puffed out his chest

rows.text: You're the biggest cow of all.
rows.note: "cow" = a dull fool, said to a man

rows.text: he always got such a kick out of working the word "aware" into that sentence twice.
rows.note: "aware" used twice, playfully

rows.text: the problem is with the receiver; the transmitter can't fix it.
rows.note: the friend's poor eyesight is the "receiver"

rows.text: I mean Alain Dickon. Diiick.
rows.note: the rude part of the pun, drawn out

rows.text: If you're Hooman, then I'm Susan.
rows.note: the gentle name Hooman doesn't suit such a hairy man

rows.text: The derivative? Meaning? Or the meaning of the derivative? Or the derivative of meaning?
rows.note: mock-profound wordplay

rows.text: God willing, may you always be araasteh.
rows.note: a blessing that puns on the surname Arasteh; araasteh = "neat"

rows.text: I can't see anything without my glasses, objectively.
rows.note: the character's habit word, used everywhere

groups.title: Children's speech
groups.q: These lines are spoken by children. Does each one sound like a child?

rows.text: – This is even better than Stadio delle Alpi.
– Pfff, donkey, who knows better, the friend of the cousin of our brother-in-law's master craftsman who is the richest man in Tehran, or you, you calf?
– Sure, you come on the mission too, but you have to be really careful. The stages are really hard.
– Okay, put less. But not too much less. A little less.
– Stage three is an intersection. An intersection means really big. From this side all the way to that side. From this street to that street.
– If you get tired, don't come on the mission anymore.
– Lots of people fail here. They go left.
– The left side is dangerous. The house with the red door belongs to a really angry old man. Even angrier than Baba.
– Our school is at the end. The last house. If we make noise, the teacher will hit our hands with a ruler.
– On the other side of the school is the cemetery. It's really old. Some of the gravestones are gone. You can see the bones of the dead.
– Hey, why did you throw away the stick? What are we supposed to ring the doorbell with, then?
– You didn't say.
– Once she learns our names she'll like us.
